name: Interview probability, set 2
description: Interview probability: dice, runs, stopping rules, fair coins, serial numbers, duels, circles, meetings, games, cards and urns. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Roll a fair six-sided die and a fair four-sided die, faces 1 to 4. You are paid the larger face in pounds.
items.question: What is the fair value, in pounds? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the chances that the larger face beats 0, 1, 2, and so on.

byKey.d6-only: You took the six-sided die alone. The four-sided die sometimes beats it, which adds value.
byKey.two-d6: You treated both dice as six-sided. The second die only reaches 4, so the larger face is lower.
byKey.mean-of-means: You averaged the two means. The larger face is at least each die, so it beats both means.

explain.text: The larger face is at most $k$ when both dice are, with chance $\tfrac{k}{6} \cdot \tfrac{\min(k, 4)}{4}$. The chances that it beats 0 to 5 add to (24 + 23 + 20 + 15 + 8 + 4)/24. That is 94/24 = 47/12 ≈ £3.92.

items.prose: An interviewer pays you the square of one roll of a fair ten-sided die, in pounds. Then they ask for the rule for any fair die with faces 1 to $n$.
items.question: What is the fair value of the square of one roll, as an expression in $n$?

feedback.correct: Correct. $\frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$, which is £38.50 for ten sides.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the squares $1^2, 2^2, \dots, n^2$.

byKey.mean-squared: You squared the average face. The average of the squares is larger, because squaring stretches the high faces.
byKey.no-divide: You added the squares but did not divide by the $n$ faces. Each face has chance $1/n$.

explain.text: Each face has chance $1/n$, so the value is $(1^2 + \dots + n^2)/n$. The sum of squares is $n(n+1)(2n+1)/6$, so the $n$ cancels. For ten sides that gives 11 × 21/6 = £38.50.

items.prose: A coin lands heads with chance 0.3. You flip it 12 times. A run is a block of equal faces in a row, so HHTH has three runs.
items.question: How many runs do you expect? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the first run, then add an indicator for each gap where the face changes.

byKey.twelve-gaps: You counted 12 places where a run can change. There are only 11 gaps between 12 flips.
byKey.no-first: You counted only the changes. The first flip always starts a run, so add 1.
byKey.fair-coin: You used a change chance of 1/2. With heads at 0.3, neighbours differ with chance 2 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.42.

explain.text: Each of the 11 gaps starts a new run when its flips differ, with chance 2 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.42. The first flip always starts a run. So the expected count is 1 + 11 × 0.42 = 5.62.

items.prose: Roll a fair twelve-sided die, faces 1 to 12, and be paid the face in pounds. After the first roll you may pay £1 to roll once more. If you do, you must keep the second roll.
items.question: What is the game worth with the best rule, in pounds? Give two decimal places.

widget.accept: 181/24 ≈ £7.54: keep 6 to 12, pay to roll again on 1 to 5.
widget.label: Value in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each first roll with the value of a paid roll.

byKey.no-reroll: You never rolled again. A first roll of 1 to 5 is worth less than the £5.50 a paid roll brings.
byKey.free-reroll: You left out the £1 cost. A paid roll is worth 6.50 − 1 = £5.50.
byKey.keep-seven: You rolled again on a 6. A 6 beats the £5.50 a paid roll is worth, so keep it.

explain.text: A paid roll is worth 6.50 − 1 = £5.50, so keep 6 to 12 and roll again below 6. Kept faces average 9 and come up with chance 7/12. So the game is worth 7/12 × 9 + 5/12 × 5.50 ≈ £7.54.

items.prose: Three red and two black cards are shuffled and turned over one at a time. Each red pays £1 and each black costs £1. You may stop at any moment and keep your total.
items.question: What is the game worth with the best stopping rule, in pounds? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Value each position from the end back. Stopping is worth 0; going on is the card plus the next value.

byKey.turn-all: You turned every card, or stopped as soon as you were ahead. Both give only £1, the reds less the blacks.
byKey.tie-zero: You valued two red and two black left at 0. Turning on there is worth 2/3, so keep going.

explain.text: Let $V(r, b)$ be the value with $r$ reds and $b$ blacks left. Working back, $V(2, 2) = \tfrac23$ and $V(3, 1) = \tfrac94$. So $V(3, 2) = \tfrac35(1 + \tfrac23) + \tfrac25(-1 + \tfrac94) = 1.5$, or £1.50.

items.prose: A bent coin lands heads with chance 1/5. You need one fair 50-50 call. Flip it twice: HT means heads, TH means tails, and on HH or TT you start again.
items.question: How many flips do you expect to make? Give two decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that one round of two flips is kept.

byKey.pairs: You counted rounds, not flips. Each round uses two flips.
byKey.one-pair: You assumed the first pair always settles it. It settles only with chance 2 × 1/5 × 4/5 = 0.32.
byKey.one-order: You counted only HT. TH also settles a round, so it is kept with chance 0.32, not 0.16.

explain.text: A round is kept on HT or TH, with chance 2 × 1/5 × 4/5 = 0.32. So you expect 1/0.32 = 3.125 rounds of two flips. That is 6.25 flips.

items.prose: Raffle tickets are numbered 1 to $N$, and $N$ is unknown. Five tickets are drawn without replacement. The largest number you see is 84.
items.question: What is the unbiased estimate of $N$? Give one decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add one average gap to the largest number seen.

byKey.max-only: You quoted the largest number seen. It sits below $N$ on average, so add a gap.
byKey.no-minus-one: You added 84/5 but left out the −1. The gaps below 84 hold 84 − 5 numbers, not 84.
byKey.k-minus-one: You shared the unseen numbers over 4 gaps. Five tickets cut the numbers below the largest into 5 gaps.

explain.text: Below 84 lie 84 − 5 = 79 unseen numbers, spread over 5 gaps. One average gap, 79/5 = 15.8, sits above the largest too. So the estimate is 84 + 15.8 = 99.8.

items.prose: Roll two fair dice. A friend looks and tells you that at least one die shows a 4.
items.question: What is the chance the dice total 9? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the rolls with at least one 4, then count those that total 9.

byKey.other-die: You fixed one die at 4 and asked the other for a 5. The 4 could be on either die.
byKey.unconditional: You ignored what your friend said. Only the 11 rolls with a 4 are left.
byKey.one-order: You counted (4, 5) but not (5, 4). Both rolls hold a 4 and total 9.

explain.text: Eleven of the 36 rolls hold a 4: 6 + 6 − 1, since (4, 4) would count twice. Two of them total 9: (4, 5) and (5, 4). So the chance is 2/11 ≈ 0.18.

items.prose: A duel: A hits with chance 0.3 and fires first. B hits with chance 0.4. They take turns until someone is hit.
items.question: What is A's chance of winning? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.correct: Correct. 15/29: firing first makes the weaker shooter a slight favourite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Condition on the first round: A hits, or both miss and the duel restarts.

byKey.first-shot: You counted only A's first shot. If both miss, the duel starts again and A can still win.
byKey.share: You split the win by accuracy, 0.3/(0.3 + 0.4). Firing first is worth more than that.
byKey.b-chance: That is B's chance. A wins the other 15/29.

explain.text: Let $x$ be A's chance. A hits at once, or both miss and the duel restarts: $x = 0.3 + 0.7 \times 0.6 \times x$. So $x = 0.3/0.58 = 15/29 \approx 0.52$.

items.prose: Nine points fall independently and uniformly on a circle.
items.question: What is the chance that some semicircle holds all nine?

options.why: You fixed one point to start the half. Any of the nine can start it, and the nine cases are disjoint.
You gave the starting point a chance of a half too. Only the other eight must land in its half.
You took each point to be in a given half with chance a half. All nine must share one half.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let one point start the semicircle, going clockwise.

explain.text: Let one point start the half, going clockwise: the other eight land in it with chance $(1/2)^8$. Any of the nine can start it, and only one can. So the chance is 9/256 ≈ 0.035.

items.prose: Draw independent uniform numbers on [0, 1] and add them up. Stop as soon as the total exceeds 1.5.
items.question: How many draws do you expect to make?

options.why: You divided 1.5 by the average draw, 1/2. The total overshoots 1.5 when you stop, so the count averages more than 3.
You scaled the answer for passing 1 by 1.5. The count does not grow in proportion to the target.
You used the corner volume $1.5^n/n!$ for every $n$. That formula holds only for totals up to 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let $m(t)$ be the expected draws to pass $t$, and start from $m(t) = e^t$ up to 1.

explain.text: Let $m(t)$ be the expected draws to pass $t$, so $m(t) = e^t$ up to $t = 1$. After a first draw $x$, $t - x$ remains, so $m(t) = 1 + \int_{t-1}^{t} m(u)\,du$ and $m'(t) = m(t) - m(t - 1)$ for $t > 1$. That solves to $m(t) = e^t - (t - 1)e^{t-1}$, so $m(1.5) = e^{1.5} - 0.5e^{0.5} \approx 3.66$.

items.prose: Two traders each arrive at a uniform time in the same 40-minute window, independently. Each waits 12 minutes for the other, then leaves.
items.question: What is the chance they meet? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Draw both arrival times as a point in a square and shade where they meet.

byKey.linear: You used 12/40 alone. Meeting is a band around the diagonal of a square, not a strip of a line.
byKey.double: You added both waits, 24/40. Take off the overlap, (12/40)² = 0.09, to get 0.51.
byKey.complement: That is the chance they miss. Take it from 1.

explain.text: Put the two arrival times on a 40 by 40 square. They miss in two corner triangles, which fit together as a 28 by 28 square: $(28/40)^2 = 0.49$. So they meet with chance 1 − 0.49 = 0.51.

items.prose: A pile holds 27 stones. Players take turns to remove 1, 2, 3 or 4 stones. Whoever takes the last stone loses.
items.question: Should you go first or second, and what is your first move?

options.why: You played as if the last stone wins. Here you want to leave one more than a multiple of 5.
A pile of 27 is not one more than a multiple of 5, so the mover can win.
You used steps of 4, as for takes of 1 to 3. With takes up to 4, the losing piles step by 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work up from small piles: a pile of 1 loses for the player to move.

explain.text: A pile of 1 loses for the mover, who must take the last stone. Each step of 5 keeps that: 6, 11, 16, 21 and 26 also lose. From 27, take 1 to leave 26, then answer each take of $t$ with $5 - t$.

items.prose: Shuffle a full deck of 52 cards and turn the cards over one at a time.
items.question: How many red cards do you expect to see before the first ace? Give one decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask, for one red card that is not an ace, the chance it comes before all four aces.

byKey.red-aces: You counted all 26 red cards. The two red aces are aces, so only 24 red cards can come first.
byKey.all-cards: That is every card before the first ace. Only half of those 48 non-aces are red.
byKey.four-gaps: You split the reds over 4 gaps. Four aces cut the other cards into 5 gaps.

explain.text: Each of the 24 red non-aces is equally likely to sit in any of the 5 gaps between aces. So each comes before all four aces with chance 1/5. The expected count is 24/5 = 4.8.

items.prose: An urn starts with 3 red and 2 blue balls. After each draw, you return the ball with one more of its colour.
items.question: What is the chance of exactly two reds in the first three draws? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance of one order, red, red, blue, then count the orders.

byKey.no-reinforce: You kept the red chance at 3/5 every draw. Each ball drawn adds one more of its colour.
byKey.one-order: You found one order, red, red, blue. There are three orders, each with chance 4/35.
byKey.at-least-two: You added three reds as well. Exactly two leaves out red, red, red.
byKey.no-replacement: You drew without returning the balls. Here each ball goes back with one more of its colour.

explain.text: Red, red, blue has chance 3/5 × 4/6 × 2/7 = 4/35. Every order gives the same product, since the same factors just swap places. Three orders give 12/35 ≈ 0.34.
